# Text-to-speech model comparison

Bee Box can speak its chat replies aloud. The voice comes from a
text-to-speech model, and the box can use more than one. New speech models
ship often, so choosing one is a recurring decision. This page holds a
comparison made for that decision, rendered on 2026-10-24: nineteen models
read the same nine short texts, and every take is here to listen to.

The box now speaks with OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts by default, or with Gemini
3.8 Flash-Lite TTS, which takes the speaking style of the box's personality.
Both were rendered through the box's own speech service, so their takes are
what the box sends.

Each take has a reference such as `R-directed-gemini38lite`: the clip's
letter, the variant, and the model. The reference is printed above the
player, and a link to `#R-directed-gemini38lite` opens the page at that take.

<!-- contents -->

## The models

<!-- models -->

Each model used one voice from its provider's standard list, named above. A
different voice of the same model can sound quite different, so a take shows
the model with that voice, not the model at its best. Cost per minute comes
from every take on this page. For models reached through OpenRouter, it is
the amount OpenRouter billed. For the others, it is the list price applied
to what was sent: characters, or for Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.1 on Google's
API, the token counts the API returned. The box service does not report
tokens, so the Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite cost is estimated from the length of the
speech.

## How it was tested

Each model read nine texts. Each text tests one thing a voice for the box
must do:

- **S, sarcasm:** words that mean the opposite of what they say. Nothing in
  the text marks it, so only direction can make it sound sarcastic.
- **A, anger held in check:** a mood the words already carry, to hear whether
  the model finds it without help, and what direction adds.
- **R, staying late:** a short "yes" that the direction asks to sound
  reluctant. The words alone sound willing.
- **L, a list in Markdown:** bullets, as Markdown. The box tries to keep
  Markdown out of what it speaks, but this test gives the model Markdown, to
  hear whether the bullets are read aloud.
- **C, code-switching on look-alike words:** a Spanish phrase and a German
  phrase that are spelled like English words.
- **D, dialog:** narration with three quoted lines.
- **E, worked math:** a short explanation that corrects a mistake, plain and
  with Markdown underscores around the word that carries the stress.
- **W, water boiling:** a denser explanation with units, numbers, and an
  aside in parentheses.
- **X, word stress:** one sentence whose meaning changes with the stressed
  word. Two variants ask for stress on "she" and on "money" in prose; one
  marks "she" with Markdown asterisks.

Every model read every text **plain**: the text alone, with no direction.
Models read the Markdown variants (L, the E and X italics) as they are, with
no direction. A model that takes direction also read the **directed**
variants, through the channel it has. Each backend takes direction in its
own way, so the directed takes are not one experiment repeated. Under each
directed take, the page shows exactly what was sent. When a model has no
channel for a variant's direction, the page says so in place of a take. The
channels:

- **A prose instruction in a separate field.** OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts
  (`instructions`) and Gemini 3.8 (`speech_metadata.style`). The direction is
  not part of the text, so the model cannot read it aloud. These models read
  every directed variant. tts-1-hd takes no instructions.
- **Prose or tags inside the text.** Gemini 3.1 takes a prose direction in
  front of the text, with free-form bracket tags such as `[sarcastically]`
  in it. Neither of its routes has a field for direction: Google's API
  rejects `speech_metadata` for 3.1, and OpenRouter's `instructions` field
  has no effect on it. ElevenLabs v3 and Fish Audio take free-form bracket
  tags, so they read the variants that have a tagged form (not the word
  stress variants). Direction inside the text can be read aloud as words.
- **A value from a fixed list.** Cartesia (`generation_config.emotion`, with
  speed and volume), MiniMax (an emotion option), and MAI-Voice-2 through
  OpenRouter (a `style`). One value applies to the whole take, and only some
  clips have a value that fits: MAI has a style only for anger. Cartesia
  accepts any emotion value without an error, and OpenRouter accepts any
  MiniMax option, so for these two a request with no effect gives no error.
  Voxtral takes fixed `[emotion=…]` and `[pace=…]` tags inside the text.
- **Events and spans.** Grok takes pauses, sighs, and spans such as
  `<slow>…</slow>` and `<soft>…</soft>`, but no emotion. It read the anger,
  staying-late, and dialog variants.
- **Nothing.** Deepgram Aura-2 and Flux and ElevenLabs Flash take no
  direction, so they read only the plain and Markdown variants. ElevenLabs
  Flash reads bracket tags aloud. Flux infers delivery from the text by
  design.

Some controls were not tried: Azure's full SSML for MAI-Voice-2 (not
reachable through OpenRouter), ElevenLabs voice settings and pronunciation
dictionaries, Cartesia pronunciation dictionaries and inline SSML-like tags,
and Voxtral's `expressiveness` and `phoneme_hints`.

**The staying-late direction.** Clip R was chosen in a listening test on
2026-10-24, in which the boxholder heard the models with an instruction
field read it with four different wordings of the reluctant direction.
Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite carried the reluctance in all four. gpt-4o-mini-tts
carried it well in none. Those takes are not on this page. The full run's takes of
clip R are under [R · Staying late](#r-staying-late), so the difference can
be heard with the wording used here.

**The transcript check.** Every take was sent to a speech-to-text model,
OpenAI's gpt-4o-transcribe. Its transcript was searched for two kinds of
extra words. Words of the direction that are not in the text mean the model
read its direction aloud. Words such as "dash", "bullet", "underscore", and
"asterisk" mean it read Markdown aloud. The other differences between
transcript and text are not shown: nearly all were the transcriber's ("3"
for "three", the foreign phrases respelled).

The renders, the transcript check, and the script that rendered every take
are in the repository at
[research/tts-model-comparison](https://github.com/ianb/beebox/tree/main/research/tts-model-comparison).

## Direction or Markdown read aloud

Direction or Markdown inside the text can be spoken as words. The
transcript check found it in these takes. The check sees only words the
transcriber wrote down, so a tag or a mark read aloud in a way the
transcriber dropped is not listed.
